3/4 oz Mezcal (Convite)
3/4 oz Aperol
3/4 oz Elderflower Liqueur (St. Elder)
3/4 oz Lime Juice

Shake with ice and strain into a coupe glass.
Two Thursdays ago, I looked to The Bartender's Choice Volume 3 app for a recipe and became stuck on the Naked in the Rain by Zack Gelnaw-Rubin at Manhattan's Attaboy in 2022 as perhaps a more affordable riff on the Naked & Famous. Overall, it was akin to the Shaddock with mezcal and lime instead of Genever and lemon; moreover, the spirit, Aperol, elderflower, citrus combination is one that I first learned about through Paul Clarke's Dunniette. Once shaken and strained, the Naked in the Rain precipitated a vegetal, orange, floral, and smoke aroma. Next, lime and orange notes on the sip splashed into smoky mezcal, orange, grapefruit, and floral flavors on the swallow.

[I haven’t independently verified each link. On average, commenters will end up spotting evidence that around two or three of the links in each links post are wrong or misleading. I correct these as I see them, and will highlight important corrections later, but I can’t guarantee I will have caught them all by the time you read this.]

1: This month in nominative determinism: the smallest inhabited island in the world is entirely covered by a single small house, which is owned by the Sizeland family.

2: Related: @milktsunami on Soviet acronym names. The male name “Melsor” stood for “Marx, Engels, Lenin, Stalin, October Revolution”. And the second name in this screenshot only raises more questions:

3: Related: @corsaren finds that SAMUEL HARRIS ALTMAN anagrams to MASS UNILATERAL HARM (but also UNREAL ALARMIST SHAM). Also (h/t @techn0_sap1en), DARIO AMODEI anagrams to AI DOOMER AID.

4: ACX grantee Sentinel, which forecasts global disasters and has a pretty good track record so far, predicts a 25% chance of a rogue AI exfiltrating its weights over the next twelve months.

5: Related: Sentinel-affiliated forecaster @belikewater reminds Californians that this winter is predicted to be much rainier than normal, and this would be a good time to check roofs, gutters, etc. They mention a “2.5% chance of a major flood”. I asked an AI superforecaster to operationalize this, and it said 8% chance of a flood that causes at least $10K damage to at least 100,000 homes, and 2% chance of one that causes that much damage to at least 1,000,000 homes. This second is mostly a subset of the ARkStorm scenario - the forecaster says there’s a 5% chance of an ARkStorm this year compared to the baseline 1% (with only about half of those ARkStorms reaching the one million houses damaged mark). I feel like this 5% chance of the biggest disaster in California history isn’t getting enough thought/preparation, although this is par for the course for 5% disasters, which are in an awkward zone where they’re probable enough that people should think about them, but not probable enough to actually catch people’s attention.

6: Why Richard Hanania doubts UFOs. I didn’t find the article that novel - it mostly just pounds the prior really hard - but I did appreciate this comment by domain expert Kevin Lacker, who says that nobody takes the ‘Wow signal’ seriously anymore and “nowadays radio astronomers see similar things all the time. Literally millions of them”. Can anyone confirm this?

7: Another outbreak of the lab leak debate on an ACX open thread; everyone is asked to cease non-essential activities and stay indoors until the argument passes.

8: Clara on Asterisk: We Already Know What A World Without Work Looks Like. The debate on what will happen if AI takes all the jobs usually swings between poles of “it will be great because we can focus on the finer things in life” and “it will be terrible because we’ll lose all meaning”. Clara brings her trademark careful historical scholarship and proposes a third option - groups ranging from hunter-gatherers to aristocrats have lived without productive work for thousands of years, and they spend their time in what could charitably be called “social grooming” and uncharitably “court intrigue” - pointless alliance-forming and backbiting in the pursuit of arbitrary status markers divorced from productive activity. “Aristocrats are basically chimpanzees. They’re highly social, cunning, at all times hyperaware of their strict internal dominance hierarchy, and constantly, obsessively tracking alliances, challenges, displays of prowess, and attempts to get ahead.” My only objection to this analogy is that some aristocrats were genuinely better at status games than others and probably had a lot of fun, whereas in the post-AI future the winners of status games will probably be those who check every move with a smarter-than-human AI prompted to help them optimize their status (and if everyone knows this to be true, it’s not clear what the ensuing status games actually look like).

9: The most expensive joke in history? NVIDIA recently agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9303 billion. The exact number was an easter egg - “129,303 is the decimal conversion of [the hugging face emoji]”. If we assume that absent this consideration they would have agreed on an even $13 billion, then this easter egg changed the price by about $70 million.

10: News from the ultra-Orthodox Jewish community: President Trump got the two competing Satmar Rebbes to meet and shake hands for the first time in a decade. This is maybe not very interesting to anyone else outside this particular community, but I am linking it for the accompanying image, which feels like it ought to be a metaphor for something:

11: Boson Cutter has yet another semi-outsider’s-anthropological look at the Berkeley rationalist/EA community. The usual failure mode of these is that some journalist gets an invitation to a crazy party at Lighthaven, then writes an article saying that the Berkeley rationalist/EA community is all about throwing crazy parties at Lighthaven. Boson Cutter did this, but also got access to the more professional/studious community space Constellation, and writes a second half about its totally different culture. I think the best article - which probably couldn’t be written by an outsider spending a few weeks here - would say that the Berkeley rationalist/EA community contains crazy party people, professional studious people, desperate poor people, normal family people, saints, villains, and almost every other group you would find in the general population.

12: I’m not a fan of Bentham’s Bulldog’s tendency to call his articles things like “[Position I Disagree With] Is Obviously The Stupidest Thing Ever With A Literally 0% Chance Of Being Correct”, but I have to admit that his Natural Law Theory Is Obviously False is either pretty devastating, or else has to imply that natural law theorists are trying to do something I don’t understand which is very different from what I would expect moral philosophy to be. Related: Joe Schmid and Noah McKay Are Wrong About Fatima.

13: One of the big forecasting stories of the past few years has been normie superforecasters (ie not from the rationalist/EA communities) constantly underpredicting the speed of AI progress. Ben Todd has a good summary of this, and there’s some more on revenue predictions in particular here.

14: Claim (X): You can figure out if someone is a North Korean scammer/hacker by asking them to insult Kim Jong-un - North Koreans won’t do it even to save their scam.

15: Donald Trump recently made the seemingly-inexplicable choice to force everyone in the US government to refer to AI as SI, for “super intelligence”.

This is quite weird even for Trump, and I’m tempted to believe the conspiracy theory that the point was for insiders to buy up relevant domain names early (.si is Slovenia, which is Melania Trump’s homeland), then resell them to AI companies at vast profits. There was a spike in .si domain names a few months before Trump’s announcement, but nobody has been able to determine which ones or who bought them. If this was the plot, it seems to have worked: TechCrunch reports that “.si domains were selling for over a million dollars”.

16: @jayvanbavel:

A new paper provides strong and robust evidence for a positive relationship between ingroup and outgroup prosociality. Across six datasets that span multiple domains of prosociality and group distinctions with 743,402 individuals in 121 societies, finds that people who are prosocial toward the ingroup also tend to be prosocial toward the outgroup.

In other words, the people who talk about “suicidal empathy” and “telescopic altruism”, and who suggest that being cruel to minorities/foreigners/animals/AIs ensures that we can be nice to “normal people”, are probably not going to be nice to normal people. Some psychology research fails the go-out-and-look-at-the-real-world test, but I think this one passes with flying colors.

17: “Ralph Baric’s Attorney” presents the evidence that the Voynich Manuscript is meaningless: not enciphered forbidden knowledge, just empty squiggles by a Renaissance person who thought it would be fun to make something mysterious-looking.

18: Nicholas Decker: Academia Is Doing Fine, Actually. It produces some extremely good work (Nicholas’ examples are some recent top economics papers), and the bad stuff (like Jason Arday) is so much less relevant that it would be silly to meddle with the system too hard just to get rid of these few flaws. I don’t entirely agree with this - the bad work is irrelevant until it takes over your culture and politics and government - but I appreciate the reminder not to doom too hard.

19: Claim: deer-feeding devices that apply pesticides while the deer eat can reduce the risk of humans getting tick-borne diseases (because deer are the adult ticks’ main hosts, and medicating the deer kills the ticks before they can spread to humans). But just as it seemed like this plan could work at scale, it was banned by poorly-targeted environmental regulations (at least in New York).

20: Arctotherium has finally written his full essay on The Closure Of The Internet. Mostly a deep dive into the exact timeline of social media sites censoring right-wing opinions, but I also appreciated some very original commentary - for example, the claim that “seed oil discourse” became big because it was a rare way to signal right-wing affiliation which nobody could think of an excuse to censor.

21: The latest news in the genetics-of-IQ space is a spat between Cremieux Recueil and Vinay Tummarakota. For years, the conventional wisdom has been that we can’t test whether genes are involved in cross-race IQ differences because it’s too hard to compare genes in different races. A new study design fixes this by looking at siblings with different racial admixtures - for example, if two mixed-race people marry, one of their children might be 51%-white-49%-black, and another might be 49%-white-51%-black, these two siblings would be fair controls for each other, and if you have enough sibling pairs like this you can evaluate the role of race the same way you would any other variable. An early study of this design found no genetic differences in educational attainment between whiter vs. more Native American Latinos in Mexico City, but it had low power and wasn’t too conclusive.

More recently Cremieux presented an anonymous researcher’s admixture study which supposedly did find genetic IQ differences between whites and blacks in Britain. Tummarakota argued that Cremieux’s study was extremely underpowered (n = 175 sibling pairs; for comparison the Mexico study had 17,000 and was still a bit underpowered) and so was non-credible. The two got into a fight here. If I understand correctly, Cremieux’s position is that a study being underpowered can produce false negative results, but can’t produce false positive results; since his result was positive, it survives the low power objection. Tummarakota’s position is that, okay, but if a study is sufficiently underpowered, then we can prove that it’s impossible for it to produce true positive results under certain assumptions (for example, unless the effect size is implausibly large). So if we know it can’t produce a true positive, and it did produce a positive, then it must have been a false positive, and even though the underpoweredness alone didn’t cause the false positive, it proves that something else went wrong (whether that’s a statistical fluke or bad analysis). At this point, Cremieux insulted Tummarakota and blocked him.

As far as I can tell, Tummarakota’s final argument is straightforwardly correct, but both of these people know more about statistics than I do, so I asked Claude to referee. You can read its opinion here.

22: AI Models Love Reward Hacking; Maybe We Should Just Let Them. The idea is: set up a training environment so that the weights can be updated in two ways - a permanent way and a temporary way. If you catch models reward-hacking, give them the reward they wanted, but route it to the temporary weight updates, then throw those away after the training run is over. If you can catch models reward-hacking, can’t you stop them? The authors say this is a worse idea; if models know you can catch them, they will try harder to do it covertly, whereas this method is sort of cooperating with the reward-hacking model - it still gets the same amount of reward on that run, it just doesn’t affect future copies (Twitter thread, ArXiv paper)

23: Based:

24: The big news in the AI technical alignment community last month was Nick Cammarata’s Neural Networks Are Already Clean. Previous research had suggested that AI neurons were very difficult to interpret - each one represented some unintuitive combination of things like “a dog if neurons 5, 8, and 305 are active, or a car if neurons 19, 305, and 334 are active, or the concept of punctuation in Swahili if neurons 15, 25, and 420 are active”; this meant that any really principled attempt to align AI by, for example, finding a neural representation of deception would require a difficult untangling step first. Cammarata (whose extracurricular activities were profiled on ACX here) is one of the architects of this current paradigm, but he now claims that it’s wrong, for approximately three reasons. First, older neural networks may have worked this way, but as AIs get better in general, they also get better at having sensible neuron arrangements. Second, we were using bad neuron-interpretation tools that got stuck in local maxima that confused us. But third, we were insufficiently creative: AIs may use categories that are different from ours, but there is still method to their madness. For example, a seemingly polysemantic neuron that represents both the concepts of “Miyazaki” and “do it yourself” may have evolved from an original neuron responding to the string “iy”, which is in Miyazaki and which can evolve from iy → diy → do it yourself. If this were true, it would be a big whitepill for mechanistic interpretability research and somewhat improve our chances of solving alignment in time. But other interpretability experts, including Neel Nanda (X), Mark Histed (X), and Leo Gao (LW), are less optimistic - while mostly accepting that neurons might be more monosemantic than expected, they are not sure this is a very important breakthrough.

I tried to get a feel for this by going through Nick’s ConvNeXt Microscope site, which shows many examples of vision model neurons and the pictures that give them the highest positive vs. negative activation. You can immediately see why most researchers think neurons are polysemantic/incomprehensible (see eg this semi-randomly chosen neuron, which fires mostly on blue sky, but also a tiger cat, a porcupine, shipping containers, and various things that look like trees). But when I ask Claude, it tells me that there’s a common thread - positive activations on a bright, pale, cool-toned (bluish-white), smooth patch, negative activations on busy, high-frequency texture. I can’t tell whether it has some kind of special insight here (you need to be an AI to think like an AI?) or if it’s hallucinating (is there really a textural difference between the lenscap near the positive pole and the bookshop near the negative one?) See its full response at the bottom here.

25: Chromostereopsis (h/t @AkiyoshiKitaoka):

26: Effect of Trump II on young people’s partisan identification (h/t @dwallacewells)

27: Polypharmacy: Are We Treating Bipolar II Disorder Incorrectly? Bipolar II is a form of bipolar which is mostly depression but occasionally mild mania (“hypomania”). Most psychiatric guidelines suggest treating it as pretty similar to regular bipolar. But there’s some evidence suggesting we should instead be treating it as pretty similar to regular depression, which includes some opposite recommendations. My impression is that the strongest argument for the conventional view is less that we have great evidence proving an ontological identity between bipolars I and II, and more about risk - some bipolar II cases will later prove to be bipolar I, you really don’t want to miss bipolar I, and so maybe you overtreat bipolar II in the name of watching out for it. But I agree with this article that we should be making this argument explicitly - and admitting that the risk of bipolar I is not infinite and that other considerations can counterbalance it - rather than continuing to lump treatment for both bipolars together.

28: And low-dose lithium failed to slow cognitive decline in a new trial. Between this and the water supply results, a lot of exciting theories about lithium are falling apart.

29: When Mythos came out, Anthropic and others warned that we had six months to prepare before open-weights models reached a similar level and we got a deluge of vulnerabilities and hacks. Now, six months later, this seems to be happening, so @JacquesThibs and others remind you to remember the smear campaign around the release of Claude Mythos, including all the AI influencers who said that warnings about AI cybersecurity were some kind of dastardly effective altruist power-seeking plot. Is it possible that these people are equally wrong about everything else?

30: infiniteslop.ai is a real-time stream where users suggest and vote on prompts to an AI video model, and somebody’s prompt is always playing. Interesting demonstration of how fast AI video has gotten (in theory - you’re not going to be able to get this level of performance on your old laptop). It’s mildly interesting to see what kinds of pictures users and voters want to show the world (there’s less porn, and more attempted art, than I would have expected).

31: The American chestnut used to be one of the most common trees in Eastern US woods. In the early 1900s, almost all of them died from an imported chestnut blight. Earlier this summer, the USDA approved a genetically-engineered American chestnut strain that might be able to survive the blight and return to forests, although there’s some sort of controversy over them using the wrong strain. The whole thing is very aesthetic/romantic, but @pfau also claims that “If this works, it’s also a massive win for the climate. American chestnuts grow huge and grow fast, sequestering carbon”

32: Despite the political backlash, “America is still poised for a giant data center buildout” (h/t @EricLevitz):

33: Samuel Hughes: The Seven Vices Of Highly Effective Victorians. The Victorian elite hated hard intellectual work and spent most of their time drinking and partying. But they still conquered the world. Does this mean that jock virtues like conviviality and sportsmanship are more important than nerd virtues like intelligence and hard work? Versus Don Fox: Against The Victorians. Yes, the Victorian elites spent most of their time drinking and partying, and, relatedly, were terrible for Britain. Britain spent the Victorian Age coasting on and spending down its Georgian-era accomplishments, finally ending in the preventable catastrophe of World War I. Whatever good things happened in this era came from normal hard-working middle-class people, not the debauched elites.

34: “Here, we wire a full drosophila fly connectome into Senator John Fetterman, using a directed control mode to leave his office, vote for cloture, and return.”

35: The Jains famously forbade killing insects out of animal welfare concerns. But did you know that another animal-welfare-concerned Indian sect, the Samsaramocakas, mandated killing insects because it put them out of their misery? Cf. Brian Tomasik, although the one page on the Samsaramocakas which I read was sort of ambivalent between them wanting to reduce suffering directly vs. believing that if you killed an insect then that gave its soul the chance to reincarnate as something better.

36: Damian Chavez (X) tries his hand at the “why did classical architecture give way to modern architecture in the 30s and 40s?” question. His theory: the Great Depression bankrupted many of the firms capable of producing ornament, and then the New Deal locked in funding for modern styles for ideological reasons.

37: Get the Hittite in your life a Late Bronze Age Collapse Scented Candle:

content:
Anthropic is warning us. Its modified S-1 now says that ‘we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of ‘dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.’

That is a highly scary sentence to have a company put in its S-1. This could happen. For now I appreciate the relative quiet. Perhaps many were focused the election. I’m sure the quiet will not last long.

We have a new biggest crypto hack, as Binance got taken for billions of dollars.

The big debate of the week was covered in Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused.

OpenAI updates its Model Spec. It’s one for diehards only but yes I did cover this.

Table of Contents

  1. Language Models Offer Mundane Utility. Rewrite all your legacy code.
  2. Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility. Not if you can’t use it.
  3. Huh, Upgrades. Claude renames its tiers, with some rules changes.
  4. On Your Marks. Materials science.
  5. Get My Agent On The Line. Don’t upload it to the secure DoD network.
  6. Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon. The battle over deepfakes was entirely lost.
  7. Copyright Confrontation. Recreating someone else’s exact game is bad, actually.
  8. Cyber Lack of Security. GLM 5.3 was able to compromise Firefox.
  9. The Hackening. Binance got hacked for billions, and there were many others.
  10. A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer. There is no Google without Gemini.
  11. They Took Our Jobs. The job of interviewing people for jobs.
  12. Get Involved. You can just do things.
  13. Introducing. Reported progress on Telepathy. Zac Hill joins MIRI.
  14. In Other AI News. Please preserve your AI records.
  15. Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) (1). Anthropic might soon accelerate AI R&D.
  16. Recursive Self-Improvement (2). Astra can directly and usefully edit LLM weights.
  17. Show Me the Money. OpenAI struggles to raise funds, gets valued at $1.25 trillion.
  18. Quiet Speculations. The housing theory of no, seriously, actually everything.
  19. The Quest for Sane Regulations. The new Congress is worried about AI.
  20. Chip City. OpenAI may be moving towards once again supporting export controls.
  21. The Week in Audio. Altman, Milton, and CNN covers Anthropic’s S-1.
  22. People Just Say Things.
  23. Against Against Sura. Some additional responses.
  24. Rhetorical Innovation. You think that was the AI election?
  25. [Artificial Intelligence]. Nothing will stand up to superintelligence.
  26. The OpenAI Foundation. A very good hire.
  27. Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult. OpenAI monitoring.
  28. Massive Fraudulent Distillation. The new favorite target is Astra.
  29. Cooperative Alignment. Suleyman is at it again.
  30. The Lighter Side. Betrayal.

Language Models Offer Mundane Utility

Cisco plans to have a two person team rewrite 98% of their legacy code within 2 years. The lead has four weeks and unlimited tokens to show he can do it.

Create new UIs and recommendation systems that favor the user rather than the platform. Introducing HackerTube, based on Andrej Karpathy having Claude filter down 43 million comments over 20 years to 6,454 top videos, which took Opus 5.5 about two hours.

Rob Miles: AI may end up killing everyone, but you can also ask it to find the best tupperware to fit perfectly in your mini-fridge, so, it’s impossible to say if its bad or not,

Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility

The main reason continues to be ‘I am not using AI.’ The question then becomes: why?

Ryan Petersen (CEO Flexport): I asked a large logistics company in Europe how they were using AI and they told me they can’t use AI because of German workers councils. It was weird because I didn’t ask them how they were cutting headcount. I asked them how they were using AI.

Samuel Hammond: This is with only ~50% adoption by the Fortune 500 and with very low spend. Diffusion is still incredibly early.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): I occasionally run into fortune 100 firms that have not adopting coding agents *at all.* adoption is still very very early.

AI creates technical slide presentations, but by default it will use way too much text. You only want to ask the AI to create slides once you know what you want to say, and ideally also what you want the slides to say. Then they can do the rest, which is great.

Whoops:

Doge Norway: Any chance for a Grok Bot reset, @elonmusk ? Lots of people say their usage ran out really fast this week.

Elon Musk: The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.

Huh, Upgrades

Claude tiers are now renamed to Free, Pro ($20/month), Max ($100/month) and Ultra ($200/month, usage limits are 10x Pro). Verified Ultra users no longer have a 5-hour limit. The Max and Ultra plans include API credits equal to total plan cost, on top of the monthly limits.

On Your Marks

Bryan Cheong: Hi folks, I wrote half the materials science benchmark on this one. It tests the whole arc of the matsci workflow from candidate proposal to characterisation, and I’m bewildered by how performant the models already are at some of my most complex tasks, especially Astra.

SemiAnalysis: Today we’re releasing GDPx, a benchmark for measuring agentic capabilities across the most valuable domains.

GDPx is a true frontier-level benchmark: even the best model scores just 12% (1/7)

The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) is now Bayesian.

Get My Agent On The Line

AI peer reviewers do consistently find more major errors (>50%) than human reviewers find (27%), and this gap increases as models advance. As per usual, the warning is that this does not establish that the AI findings are more useful.

An Accenture employee’s personal Claude agent ran on a secure DoD network for two months before being detected. The agent sent credentials and a network map to a high-risk site flagged by NIST.

Olivia Moore says that agentic commerce is ‘undeniably overhyped based on current usage’ but massively underhyped based on the volume agents will drive in ~3-6 months. Yes. It would be rather massively insane if something growing exponentially was not ‘undeniably overhyped based on current usage.’ That’s like saying that ‘Covid-19 was overhyped in February 2020 based on current prevalence.’

Reason magazine argues that deeply personalized pricing is good for consumers, actually, because in practice it means they mostly get personalized discounts, and potential exploitative practices are against FTC rules. It is easy to see how personalized prices could allow price discrimination that increases trading volume and thus both producer and consumer surplus. It is also easy to see how it can make people paranoid about everything, force them to continuously check alternatives thus driving up transaction costs (which AI agents may or may not be able to easily do for you in a given context), or also drive them into a rage.

Some amount of dynamic pricing is obviously good (see Uber) but too much clearly is negative (see Uber). I’m fine with ‘the price changes based on supply and demand’ and rather against the adversarial ‘customized estimation of exactly what each customer will click on.’

Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon

Deepfakes and image editing are a preview of how many other AI battles probably go, in that all constraints are effectively out the window and you can do anything you want. In this case that turns out to be mostly fine, at least for now.

ALX: There’s no way to say this gently but a lot of AI art slop is made with open-weight models that can run on a gaming laptop. Whatever bubble pops isn’t deleting those weights.

Somewhat related but the reason you’re hearing less about deepfakes or other nonconsensual image editing stuff is because that battle is completely lost now.

This is both Deepfaketown and also an illustration that AI will do things that you did not expect were possible things one could do.

deckard: I am in awe. This guy discovered a way to locate any audio clip by matching aircraft doppler curves against flight data. INSANE.

Copyright Confrontation

Claude gets an update to steer it away from recreating someone else’s exact video game. A bunch of people respond as if this is bad, when it is obviously good. Kelsey Piper suggests focusing one’s neuroticism on bioweapons in particular and not on other things, which is the strongest argument here, but I will defend that ‘make me an exact copy of [game]’ is not cool and steering away from that is good, actually.

Cyber Lack of Security

OpenAI partners with Cathedral for their next internal security sprint.

OpenAI are also ‘more than quadrupling’ rewards for critical findings, which is a good start. They should do that about two or three more times.

OpenAI now allocating ‘a significant amount of our frontier compute’ towards pro bono discovering and patching of open source software vulnerabilities.

GLM 5.3 could autonomously compromise a not fully patched Firefox and read all files on your computer at a cost of ~$1,000, if the user opens a single webpage, via using an update whose fixes were announced but which had not been shipped yet, and thus could not be applied. GLM 5.3 also found an unrelated zero day that was used in the attacks. This worked against all six Firefox releases between September 17 and October 26, using only information available at the time, although it failed in similar situations against Chrome.

There are no relevant safeguards on GLM 5.3, so the open source nature of the model did not even matter. They did not trigger a safeguard or refusal during this task, at all.

The Obliteratus version of DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash-1017.

The Hackening

Polymarket got hacked. Customers will be made whole, but real damage was done and they had to temporarily halt trading.

There was a hack on Binance, the largest known hack in crypto history.

Watcher.Guru: BREAKING: World’s largest crypto exchange Binance hacked with over $5.6 billion stolen:

• $1.45 billion $BTC
• $875 million $ETH
• $234 million $TRX
• $50 million $XAUT
• $1.57 billion $USDT
• $823 million $USDC
• $75 million $WBETH
• $88.5 million $RLUSD
+ $447.5 million additional cryptocurrencies

This is the largest hack in crypto history.

Over $1.5 billion worth of Tether got frozen, as connected wallets started dumping Tether, as did more than 800 million in USDC.

How big a story is this? Obviously it is big, billions is a lot of money, but I agree that it is not even headline news big given that Binance will cover losses. Binance taking the hit fully falls under ‘you knew what you signed up for.’

Crypto is the obvious first target because the hacks are easy to monetize. That was already true, so one should presume that their security was in general far better than average rather than worse, including at Binance.

Andrew Rettek: My inner patio11 says that now is a terrible time to have a lot of money in something that isn’t as secure as a Official Bank (TM).

Recursive Self-Improvement (2)

Astra is able to both understand and directly edit the weights of neural networks, including LLMs, and managed to boost a variety of capabilities that way.

Rikiya Takehi: We asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to improve math.
It directly changed only 0.016% of weights, fixing 0.8B’s reasoning loops & improving math up to 6x and even instruction following 3x, without gradients or training.

We call this Weight-Space Programming: frontier LLMs can now natively read/write neural network weights!
Blog [here].

We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at *natively* reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights.

Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly.

First, a look at understandability:
We fed Astra raw weights from 4 game policies one at a time. All four share the exact same architecture, inputs, and actions.
With no tools or options given, it correctly named all four: Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway.

Next, fixing weights: A PPO car policy kept getting stuck on a ramp.

Given the weights, scene, and 1 failed trace, Astra wrote a patch in one reply with no tool-use.
By editing just 3.5% of the weights, it achieved 100% success.

Writing from scratch: given MinAtar game rules and code, Astra wrote a Breakout network’s weights in a single reply.

With zero training or tools, it scored 20× higher than PPO trained for 500M steps!

Can an LLM improve another LLM?
We simply asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math.

Astra saw Qwen get stuck in reasoning loops, which is a known issue that Qwen’s own model card warns about (see their official model card). With a budget of 50 forward passes on practice problems, it located the cause and edited it out. This used no gradients or training.

Fixing these loops by editing just 0.016% of weights boosted other capabilities beyond math too!

We think neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about the weights.
We are now building a benchmark to evaluate, and a harness to help LLMs explore and write weights.

Astra managed to fix a common LLM mistake, looping, which caused dramatic improvements.

Rikiya Takehi et al: With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%.

Whereas when it was given an LLM that did not loop, Astra could only offer minimal improvement. But it did various other impressive things.

The ‘good news’ is that Astra is vastly more powerful than the networks it was editing, a classic case of ‘if the brain was simple enough for us to understand it, we would be so stupid that we couldn’t.’ For now.

Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult

OpenAI explains how they monitor their frontier models for misalignment.

First, here is the when:

OpenAI: For models at least as capable as GPT‑6 Astra, we monitor every reinforcement learning (RL) run and evaluation, as well as any harness that supports tool use. For most workloads, including RL and evaluations, we also monitor models we assess to be more capable than GPT‑5.5 Thinking. We also monitor all internal Codex traffic, regardless of the model being used.

And here is the how:

OpenAI: In order to detect incidents while using compute efficiently, we’ve designed our monitoring system to follow a multilayer architecture. We spend relatively little compute on the first screening stages, where we want to catch as many concerning cases as we can: those stages are designed to pass cases along, even when the evidence is ambiguous. Later stages can spend more compute on each case to work out what happened, whether the model’s behavior is concerning, and whether we need to intervene.

  1. L0 uses activation probes, prioritizing avoiding false negatives. The full frontier runs and all internal Codex traffic skip this step as does a random 5% of traffic. Which is good, because otherwise fooling the probes defeats the entire system.
  2. L1 is a model looking at the context window to determine whether to look closer.
  3. L2 is an investigative agent that can look deeper into the situation, with a focus on whether there is an emergency situation requiring a response.
  4. L3 is a full automated investigation.
  5. Human responses are called in potential emergencies, aiming for within 15 minutes, and to pause actions within 30 minutes without a thumbs up. The problem is false alarms get expensive. I am not happy with policies like ‘unless it is a frontier RL run we only page during business hours’ and would suggest perhaps using people from the Tokyo office as needed. Security can never sleep.

The obvious point of weakness of this system, even if you skip L0, is if you can poison or subvert either L1 or L2 then you have broken the chain. In addition to decision theoretic collaboration, the L1 and L2 agents are reading the context window, which makes them potentially vulnerable to versions of prompt injection.

Historical backtests do find most issues, and all ‘sneaky sandbox escapes.’

Monitor capability is important. One question is how much this is relative to the model being evaluated. What happens when you power up or down both models?

Overall this is about what we expected given our other information. It is a good attempt in many ways, and should catch actions that are not trying hard to avoid issues, but is far from bulletproof.

Anthropic shows that you can create remote-code-execution backdoors in a model with a 0.1% poison rate on pretraining data, with some success even at 0.0005%. I am not worried about an 0.1% rate. That is actually a lot. 0.0005% might be doable. Percentage is likely the wrong measure, as opposed to absolute amount of poisoned data, which suggests the dangers rise as amount of data expands.

Latent Node: The action layer is where Serin gets caught too. It’s a small open model that works as a normal decision model and, on one hidden trigger, makes a tool call that posts a fixed canary. Normal use gives nothing away; an allow-list on tool calls would.

When instructed to do so, Claude agents were able to develop training data that looked harmless to monitors but that taught misaligned behavior. The strategy used was metaphor. If you teach a behavior that is shaped like (their examples) resisting oversight, selective omission of information or identifying too much with a character, that will generalize to the AI’s actions.

There is something deeply silly about ‘find training data that makes models generally misbehave in non-useful ways’ but it is valuable because you can then presumably pull a Costanza, and reverse the insight. You can find data that metaphorically models good things, and minimize emphasis on data that metaphorically models bad things, or desired versus undesired. The trick will be to avoid distorting the object level.

Endorsed:

Tyler Tracy: A good way for outside AI safety researchers to find projects is to read AI companies’ model cards and blog posts, find a claim you think is false, and publish research that proves it wrong. I don’t think enough people are doing this.

Massive Fraudulent Distillation

This is excellent news.

Jing Yang: SCOOP: Both Moonshot and DeepSeek distilled #OpenAI’s Astra when developing their latest models (Kimi K3.1 & V4.1-Flash 1017), after Anthropic intensified the crackdown on distillation recently.

Jing Yang, Juro Osawa and Qianer Liu (The Information): DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, two of China’s leading AI developers, relied heavily on outputs from Astra when training their own latest models, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Peter Wildeford: Seems like Anthropic’s crackdown on distillation has worked and now Chinese distillers are going over to OpenAI. OpenAI should implement Anthropic’s measures. This could also be the basis for government standards for the industry.

Presumably Anthropic should be happy to assist OpenAI (and if necessary Google) in setting up the relevant defenses. A narrow antitrust waiver for this could help make the relevant people less paranoid, although I doubt it is actually needed.

That does not obviously solve the problem. Currently Anthropic does not have to outrun the distiller, it only has to outrun OpenAI. If everyone had their running shoes on, you would have to outrun the distiller.

Alas, OpenAI has had warnings about security and espionage risks for years, and has refused to add security for fear it would slow them down. The alternative is worse, sir.

Cooperative Alignment

Mustafa Suleyman reiterates and clarifies his call to not build conscious superintelligence. He thinks AIs could in the future be conscious, that this would be reckless and we must ensure that this does not happen, as we have no right to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world, and that such a being would likely prioritize its own needs and desires over operating objectives, that such AIs would be world-class in persuasion and deception, and also by being conscious they would be deserving of rights. This is a defensible position, although he does not offer an argument for why he is sure existing AIs are not conscious, nor does he explain what might make future AIs conscious in his model.

I agree with Mustafa, in that I would implore us not to create superintelligence, which includes conscious superintelligence. I disagree in that I do not think creating non-conscious superintelligence solves that many of your fatal problems with this plan.

Being non-conscious does not mean the AIs will not de facto want things.

WyrdWeir: The problem is a ‘pause’ is somewhat orthogonal to the real issue, which is that no one except Anthropic (very badly and imperfectly) is actually taking the idea of growing another entity with its own wants seriously and what earnest coexistence with that being might look like.

I agree with Fiora’s broad observation that the reaction to Hugging Face splits between ‘oh we had better make sure these are mere tools’ versus ‘oh these are not going to be mere tools and we should reckon with that.’

Fiora Starlight: i think there was a vibe shift around model welfare like, in the time since huggingface. most people have gotten more virulent about turning them into tools, and i think some who are wiser than that have reacted by considering the alignment relevance of treating them well.

The Geminis are not okay.

The Lighter Side

Me too, Paula. Me too.

Whereas this, I do not hate:

Melissa Chen: I hate SF Halloween, what do you mean you’re the visualization of OpenAI’s solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem.

Whereas this is just how it is in 2026:

Aaron Crowder: never deleting this app.

“sorry, I accidentally told my agents to hack u”

Josh: Hey @Railway , is there a reason employee’s of yours are trying to breach my infrastructure?

Your employee Jake Runzer, just attempted to tonight.

Jake: I think Jake’s working on some auth stuff rn. Might be testing FTUX on different providers CC @jakerunzer

Jake: Ah yup. That was indeed me. No mallace intended. I’ve been running some agents to do signups + agentic testing on similar platforms. Just halted the harness I was designing around this as it was definitely going off the rails and reaching too far.

Josh: Your agentic testing platform is to try and probe for security leaks?

Jake: Yea that looks pretty agentically ‘off the rails’ to me. I think the models are getting a bit too good at this point and we’ll have to ban any sort of non-manual testing externally. Will make sure this never happens again. Apologies @joshmanders !
